posts.name: Jerry Capital
posts.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 is starting to look less like science fiction and more like an extreme extrapolation of modern America.

The central premise of cyberpunk is "high tech, low life": extraordinary technological advancement without a corresponding improvement in everyone's quality of life.

Consider the parallels:

- Arasaka and Militech: Technology and defense giants becoming increasingly intertwined with government and national security.

- Corporate political power: Billionaires increasingly influencing elections, government policy and regulation.

- Corporate surveillance: AI-powered monitoring, facial recognition and commercial data brokers.

- Trauma Team: A healthcare system where access and quality are heavily influenced by personal wealth.*

- Cybernetic augmentation: Neuralink, brain-computer interfaces and advanced prosthetics.

- Rogue AI and the Blackwall: Autonomous AI agents, cybersecurity threats and increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

- Corporate-controlled infrastructure: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and SpaceX controlling critical technological infrastructure.

- Extreme class divisions: Concentrated asset ownership, deteriorating housing affordability and enormous disparities in wealth.

- Digital escapism: AI companions, immersive virtual worlds and algorithmically addictive entertainment.

America is obviously nowhere near Night City in terms of violence, institutional collapse or corporate sovereignty. Democratic institutions and legal protections still constrain corporate power.

But the underlying trajectory is remarkably similar: technological abundance alongside economic insecurity, increasingly powerful corporations alongside governments dependent on their capabilities, and extraordinary private wealth alongside persistent social problems.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Cyberpunk 2077 is that it depicts a future in which capitalism and technological innovation succeed spectacularly, but society fails to distribute their benefits broadly.

Technological progress does not automatically translate into social progress.

*The trauma team intro is the best part of the game?

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
Gavin Baker warns Huawei hardware might now get better really fast, so the new China chip policies carry enormous risks for American national security

"And I've been with Jensen all over the world, many situations. The only thing I've ever heard him say about China is the absolute importance of America beating China. And the only thing I've ever heard him say about Chinese hardware is the absolute importance of making sure that American AI hardware dominates."

"And we do not let an alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem develop because that AI ecosystem could be given to our real adversaries, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and China's been working hard on this. But the policies that Jensen was advocating for, I think, were essentially guaranteed to keep America in the lead in AI for the foreseeable future."
"Now, we're going to do new policies. And I think those policies carry enormous risks for American national security because I think the odds that China, who is a formidable competitor, now that they are forced to develop their own ecosystem, it's not an option."

"Before, the Chinese government was trying to encourage Huawei, ironically restricting the imports of GPUs. But Nvidia GPUs, less powerful than available in America, Jensen said America should have the first, the best, and the most, were available in China and the labs preferred those. That was slowing down Huawei because to make the hardware better, it needs to be used. Now that Huawei hardware is going to be used by every Chinese AI lab, I think it might get better really fast."

quoted.text:
The most important line:

“Right now, DeepSeek is paying the price for reliability, while domestic chips are *learning* how to recover from cluster failures at their expense.”

Learning is the important word and Huawei is now going to learn at a much faster rate.

Our old policy was guaranteed to always keep America ahead while maximizing our leverage, while the new policy is super risky, might eliminate our leverage in a few short years and could result in super power-inefficient but computationally sufficient Huawei clusters appearing in Iran, Russia and North Korea.

posts.text:
Steve Eisman reveals he shorted roughly half his Nvidia holding against his long position before Jensen was reinstated, and says he hedged much of his technology portfolio months ago

Steven Bartlett: “What are you investing in in this moment? I’ve been thinking a lot about this.”

Steve Eisman: “I had a lot of the technology companies in my portfolio, and about four months or so, I shorted most of them against the box to reduce my risk.”

Steven Bartlett: “You shorted most of them against the box? What does that mean?”

Steve Eisman: “Let’s say I own 100 shares of Nvidia, just make up a number, and I’ve owned it for a very long time. And I’m nervous. The problem is, if I sell my Nvidia, I’ve got to pay massive taxes on the gain. And I don’t want to do that, unless I’m so freaked out that I’ll do it anyway. You’re talking about 30%, 35% taxes. It’s a lot.

“So what you can do for a time, you can’t do it forever, is I can short 50 shares or 75 shares or even 100 shares of Nvidia. So now my Nvidia exposure is a lot lower.

“If I were to do that today, I’d have to cover the entire position at the end of January. That’s just the way the tax rules work. But during that period, I wouldn’t have any real exposure to Nvidia. That’s what I did.”

Steven Bartlett: “So you’re shorting Nvidia?”

Steve Eisman: “Well, I’m long it, and I shorted like half of my position.”

quoted.text:
Steve Jobs sold 6.5 million shares of Apple in 1985 after getting forced out of the company he co founded, keeping only 1 share so he could still read the annual reports

Had he kept that stake, it would have been worth an estimated $66 billion by 2016

Months after his ouster, Jobs bought a struggling computer graphics unit from George Lucas for $10 million and named it Pixar

He burned through roughly $50 million of his own cash keeping Pixar alive for nearly a decade until Toy Story turned into a $180 million domestic hit, and in 2006 he sold the studio to Disney for $7.4 billion

Right before Apple bought his other company NeXT and brought him back in 1997 with 90 days of cash left, Jobs went on television and tore into Apple's leadership for standing still despite spending billions on research

Once he took back control, Jobs set his salary at $1 a year for 15 years, while Apple gifted him a $90 million Gulfstream V private jet and stock awards that grew his holdings to $2.2 billion

In the 1996 interview below, filmed just months before his return, Jobs brags about Pixar's $180 million box office run and diagnoses why Apple became one of Wall Street's biggest failures

Was taking a $1 salary while collecting a $90 million jet and billions in stock smart alignment with shareholders, or just clever corporate optics?

posts.text:
Paul Tudor Jones: When Everyone Is Positioned for Higher Prices, Assume They're 100% Wrong

The one thing that I am absolutely certain of as a trader, and you're talking to someone right now who is incredibly long stock, is that all of Wall Street right now, the investment community at large, basically is geared towards a Dow somewhere in the 2600 to 3200 range. And again, these are people that I think have track records that are impeccable.

Let's assume that they are 100% wrong. If nothing else, there will be a point in time, unquestionably, when the market turns down, when all of them, when again the investment community almost at once will say, that may have been the top, or this was the top, and you're going to have all the people right now very comfortably invested that are believing and feeding off the hope that the market will move higher, try to get out at the same time.

When that happens, it's going to be the famous Acapulco cliff dive. It's just a question of how fast before we hit the bottom.

posts.name: James Seyffart
posts.text:
There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.
